Text:
A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Weekends aren’t that good..
Just lying there doing nothing until you have to get back into society. Too poor to do anything besides watch TV and play the same mediocre video games.. and every shop you want to go to is either crowded or closed… I’m not a fan..



They receive the following reply to their post:

Man, I hear you. Weekends can feel like a letdown if you can't really do much because of budget constraints or overcrowding. When I was going through a similar phase, I tried switching up small things to make weekends more enjoyable without spending much cash. Like exploring local parks or nature trails—they’re free to visit and often less crowded than city spots. Sometimes I’d go to random garage sales just to browse, maybe find a cheap book or something interesting. You also might try picking up a new hobby that you can do at home, like cooking a new dish with whatever’s in the pantry. But yeah, not having a lot of cash on hand can really suck the fun out of relaxation time. I remember I’d get pretty stir-crazy every now and then. But finding small, doable projects with what I had around seemed to help. Sometimes, I just try to remind myself it’s okay to have those weekends where not much happens. Not every weekend has to be amazing, right? It often feels like there's society-created pressure to make every weekend super exciting, when really just chilling at home is sometimes nice too. Ah, I don’t know, maybe it’s just all about perspective or something like that. Anyway, hope your weekends get better and more fulfilling, somehow.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

[feedback] I built a SaaS to automate Amazon affiliate marketing on Telegram - and to get started with Amazon Associate
I wanted to share a project I originally developed for my own use and have since turned it into a SaaS platform to help others. The service automates Amazon affiliate marketing by: * Finding discounts on Amazon, * Shortening URLs with your affiliate ID, and * Publishing deals on Telegram channels. It also includes tools for tracking product prices and notifying users when prices drop below a set threshold. *(Note: on the landing page you can find some links to the Telegram channels. Those channels are redirect to the private ones since Amazon doesn't allow sharing links on public channels.)* The service is self-sustaining for users with a decent audience. For example, €15 (Bronze tier cost) can be recouped within about a week by sharing your Telegram channel on social media or blogs [of course you need to advertise it have/found a user base]. **Who it’s for:** * Amazon Associates with a PA-API key (required for crawling Amazon). * Those starting out can use the **Platinum Plan**, which creates a ready-made website with product reviews and affiliate links. This helps you get verified as an Amazon associate, after which you can earn a PA-API key by completing sales. There’s also a free 5-day trial for the Bronze tier if you'd like to give it a try.



They receive the following reply to their post:

I get where you’re coming from, but I'd be cautious about investing heavily in this without knowing all the details. First, Amazon affiliate stuff is tricky. They've got a ton of rules and change them a lot, so I'd worry your service can suddenly get restricted or banned, especially using Telegram where things can come off a little spammy. Amazon is notorious for cracking down on associates even for the slightest rule-breaking. Also, just be careful because the whole idea of putting links in private channels might not seem super reliable to users. I remember trying out something simpler on Facebook a while ago, and reached a ton more people than I expected, so maybe think bigger than private Telegram. Social media is a game-changer but also a headache if you’re not watchful. The part of creating a ready-made website is neat though - it might attract beginners who don’t want to deal with it, but man, make sure these sites stand out. There’s a lot of cookie-cutter stuff out there. If full customization isn’t an option, at least find a way to make your pages feel unique. Basics like good SEO and easy navigation make them easy to push. People don’t just click random links anymore; they need a reason, a vibe. A free 5-day trial is okay, but make sure someone notices it before jumping in. At the end of the day, I’d still recommend thinking about what happens to folks who sign up but don't have an established audience yet. They might struggle, and having options or guidance beyond social sharing could help. It could be a great tool if all things line up, but maybe keep an eye on how you're planning on addressing those Amazon rules and how different your product looks compared to everything else out there...

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Clutter was coming back. I took control.
After two successful years decluttering and optimizing my space, in the last 2 or 3 months clutter was starting to come back. I was getting worried because I absolutely didn't want to get back to the time when I could barely breathe in my own room. Today I took control. I checked 4 out of my 6 regions (I divided my room in 6 regions) and flagged for donation some things while others were just thrown away. My room feels so much better and it'll be better once I finish the two pending regions. This exercise also helps a lot to save money. How? You can see the stuff you have accumulated and avoid unnecessary future purchases. I do not need more batteries. I do not need more shower curtains. I do not need more USB cables. I do not need more socks. I do not need more notebooks. I have enough of those things and buying more of them would be a waste. I will close this post with a phrase I heard a few years back watching a YouTube video. *The more things that you own, the more energy and time you have to spend maintaining them, storing them and keeping them organized.*



They receive the following reply to their post:

Hey, I hear ya, but I think you might be missing something. Clutter is normal. Most people have busy lives, and your environment is going to change from season to season, especially during times of transition. Sure, avoid buying more of what you already have enough of, but life doesn’t stay the same forever, and neither will your clutter. For instance, I used to be the queen of baby stuff when my kids were little. Now though, I'm just holding on to the extra stuff I have for the future. Embrace the phases! As long as you’re dedicating the time to a quarterly or even biannual clutter check, you’re ahead of the game. You’re clearly maintaining things well for the most part. And honestly, clutter sometimes equals real, lived-in, messy life, and that’s okay too. What’s organized now, likely won’t matter a week from now… It is what it is.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Sell the startup at 95% discount, give it away, or shut it down?
In July 2024, I co-founded a startup called Helpy Travel with two partners. By September, we were accepted into Bocconi 4 Innovation, the pre-acceleration program of the most prestigious business university in Italy. The product evolved into a scalable SaaS for short-term rental properties, and we gained real users and a strong sales pipeline. Fast forward to February 2025: all co-founders receive job offers from large corporates. At the same time, we receive a **1M€ valuation** and an **investment proposal of 50K€ for 5%** from the acceleration program. The team decides not to move forward. But the project is solid, the product is mature, and the market is big and niche-focused. So here’s the dilemma: * Find someone willing to take over and lead the startup? * Sell the assets (software, brand, sales pipeline) for a bunch of dollars? * Give it away to someone with the right energy and vision? * Just shut it down? What would you do?



They receive the following reply to their post:

you got a whole startup with potential and just wanna watch it go down the drain? why work that hard get into all those programs get offers from large corporates just to give it up? people spend years dreaming about building something from scratch, is like painting the Mona Lisa and then using it as a placemat. at least try selling it! see what you can get out of it. but giving it away or shutting down? that’s just lazy. if you believe in what you built, find someone who’ll take the baton—don’t just drop it. but if the corporate world is where you see your future then make sure to get something out of all the work you’ve put in! Otherwise, it’s just a waste.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Working at the sentence level: how not to write a lazy sentence
You think you’ve got a good story. Perhaps you do. So you set out to write the first draft. But remember, which I’m sure you do because it’s been told a hundred times—the first draft is always that, the first. So what are you doing in your second draft? What is revisioning? What are you revising? Perhaps the plot. A few scenes. Changing some facts about the character or a place. Then they say, revise again. What are you revising now? What I’m getting at is that at some point you have to revise at the sentence level. One of the first things my dissertation advisor told me during my Masters thesis was: this is good but your sentences are lazy. He was right. I wrote and re wrote and re wrote till all the words looked the same to me and grammar stopped making sense. But I didn’t really focus on the sentence level. By that, I mean, making sure you don’t use lazy words. Try and keep the sentences clean, clear and fresh. Here is a sentence by MacArthur Genius Aleksander Hemon from his book of essays, Book of my Life. "I WAS A NIHILIST," writes Aleksandar Hemon, "and lived with my parents. I even started thinking up an Anthology of Irrelevant Poetry, sensing that it was my only hope of ever getting anthologized." He adds, "Nothing came of it, although there was a world of irrelevant poetry everywhere around us. There was nothing to do, and we were running out of ways to do it.” https://open.substack.com/pub/bukus/p/re-working-lazy-sentences?r=9brcu&utm_medium=ios



They receive the following reply to their post:

I know what you’re talking about. It’s like, you think you’ve nailed your story, but then you look closer and your sentences are just... there, you know? I’ve been there when writing my own stuff. You kind of have to zoom in and really give those sentences a workout. I remember once I thought I’d finished an essay, and my professor just circled sentence after sentence with notes like “too vague” or “needs more punch.” It’s not about fancy words or anything. It’s about how you can make each sentence work harder to say exactly what you want it to say. One thing that helped me is reading my work out loud. You can catch a lot of lazy or awkward stuff that way. Plus, thinking about the rhythm helps too. It’s kind of like music that way, where sometimes you want the tempo to change, the beats to hit just right. Maybe try looking at sentences from authors you admire, like you mentioned Aleksandar Hemon. Seeing how they string words together can give you an idea of how to make a sentence sing. It’s a bit like practicing scales on a piano, you know? You just keep at it until it feels right. And hey, sometimes you’ve got to let a piece rest and come back to it. Things often look clearer after a little break. Anyway, that’s what works for me, but I’m sure there’s plenty more to try...

I’d actually find that super useful in a weird way! Sometimes I think my farts are silent (I called them secret assassins back in the good ol’ college days), but boy, was I wrong. So, having the power to see them would be a game-changer for knowing just when to leave the room and save face! Feels like an unusual magic trick, in a way… I’m spiraling again, aren't I?

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

You Can Turn Into Animals While Retaining Your Mass
You can turn into any animal that exists or has ever existed. Want to turn into a cat? Sure but you weigh basically the same as you do currently. Want to turn into a T-Rex? Sure but you'd probably be all flesh and (hollow) bones. What are some of the best transformations for the average person? The worst? How would you try to make this not suck?



They receive the following reply to their post:

Haha, this one made me chuckle. Imagine being a tiny cat that crashes through floors because you still weigh like, 160 pounds. Or being a T-Rex that people could just push over, because you're like, basically a balloon. But, I guess it would still be cool for short-term stuff. Like, as a bird, you'd still be able to fly briefly, right? Maybe more like those airplanes that land at very short distances—lifting off wouldn't be gentle, but you could, like, glide or something. Realistically, turning into a big animal like a rhino would actually be so awkward when you end up the size of the rhino but weighing like, 150 pounds. You'd just flop around! Maybe you'd just look at it less like becoming an animal and more like a party trick? The comedic potential is endless at parties for sure! But to make it useful, utilizing the disguise opportunities would be quite funny. Like, turning into a little duck doing reconnaissance but watching out for people trying to pick you up because they'd probably walk away with sore arms. I wonder about finding an animal that could hide weight well, maybe like a whale in water since it's mostly buoyant—then would people notice? I'm still thinking small animals would still be the funniest, like a heavy hedgehog rolling down a hill. There's a lot of good comedy potential here, for sure!

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Tips for Atlantic coastal route in Africa needed
I'm travelling with a Finnish passport so I'm wondering how to manage all the visas. Most visas seem to be either eVisas or visas on arrival so is there any problems with travelling to these countries by land? The official visa application page for Ivory Coast at least says that travel by land is not currently possible. This is my source [https://www.passportindex.org/passport/finland/](https://www.passportindex.org/passport/finland/) and it seems to be pretty accurate. If you have ever travelled the same journey from Morocco to South Africa by the Atlantic coast then all possible info is welcome, the total cost of all visas, how much time to spent in each country, recommendations, tips, etc. I won't have my own car but I'll hitchhike so info about stuff related to getting your own car through the borders is not needed. Thank you for all the help :)



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh, that sounds like an epic adventure! I haven't done the whole Atlantic coastal route myself but I've been to a few spots and know folks who have. Visas can definitely be a bit tricky when you're going overland and not just flying in and out. With your Finnish passport, it's generally easier, but there’s always a wrinkle or two when you're crossing borders by land in Africa. Like you mentioned, Ivory Coast's land border thing is a bit of a snag right now, so maybe double-check that before you get too deep into planning that part of your route. For countries with eVisas or visa on arrival, I’d say always check the latest travel forums or expat groups in each country because rules can change and not every land crossing is equal. Some border posts are more lenient or knowledgeable about visas than others. And make sure you've got physical copies of everything; a lot of places like those handy. Budgeting for visas can add up because some countries don’t shy away from high visa fees for backpackers. But yes, countries like Ghana, Nigeria, and Angola can all vary, so it's best to do a deeper dive country by country. Try to email embassies for the most updated info on visa cost—they usually respond pretty quickly. I know you won't have your own car, but with hitchhiking, just be prepared to be flexible with time—it can be unpredictable compared to driving or public transport. It's incredibly rewarding though because you’ll meet the most interesting people that way. Each stretch of the journey will likely offer something different, from the markets in Senegal to the beaches in Namibia. Oh, and quick tip: have local SIM cards or some data plan that works for multiple countries; connectivity is sometimes your best friend for checking maps or language translating apps. Can’t wait to hear about your travels—it’s gonna be wild!

The simple answer is that most of my physical media shopping is at Goodwill and I don't ever see 4K discs there. However, I would also argue that DVDs aren't bad at all, even in today's world. They receive the following reply to their post:

Man, I'm totally with you on this. DVDs aren't the shiny new toy anymore, but they still do the job. You know, there’s something comforting about just popping in a DVD and knowing you get the full movie without any interruption from internet buffering or an expired content license taking it off of Netflix, which really annoys me. I get it, 4K is all crisp with colors that jump out like they're trying to hug you or something, but sometimes all I need is to watch my favorite movie while eating a pizza and not worrying if my streaming service cuts out. Plus, DVDs sometimes come with those fun special features that streaming won't offer. Super fascinating stuff, like director's commentaries or bloopers. A lot of that gets lost when you focus only on 4K. And let's be real, my TV isn't exactly the latest model, so it doesn't even do 4K justice. Oh, and DVDs are great for road trips when you want to play something on portable players or older gadgets. Who cares if it’s not perfect picture? A user makes the following post on a social media site:

When to move on?
Hello everyone! I am currently in a writing class where I am developing a play. I am curious about how we as writers know when to transition between acts. What do we tend to expect to happen in each act? How do you map out your plot to feel like a true play instead of a long stretch of scenes?



They receive the following reply to their post:

I think the transition between acts is kind of like the rhythm of the story, right? It’s that moment when something big enough happens to shift the direction or stakes of the whole play. In my experience, each act should have its own sort of climax or peak moment that changes things for the characters. Like, something that's strong enough that if the audience left at that point, they'd still remember it. In the first act, you’re usually setting up the world and getting the audience invested in what’s at stake. The next act builds up those conflicts or obstacles, maybe throws in a twist, leading to a bigger climax. The final act typically resolves everything, but not always, because I love when there’s a few lingering questions left. As for mapping out plots, I sometimes start with bullet points of big events or emotional beats I want to hit. I try placing them like puzzle pieces until I have a flow that makes sense. It’s different for everyone though. I’ve met people who do detailed outlines and folks who write straight through and rearrange later. It’s about what helps you keep track of those turning points and keeps the tension rolling. And, of course, sometimes you just sense it allowing yourself to be flexible, you know? Anyhow, it’s also important to leave room for characters to surprise you, which makes writing fun…

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

I have a really hard time transporting my ideias to writing
Hi everyone! I know this is such a common problem with creators of any kind and area of work. My main problem when writing fanfiction is that I am an extremely visual person. What mean by this is, when I have ideas for scenes and such, I visualise them like a movie, with a specific angle, a specific shot, specific gestures and facial expressions that are often not really easy to describe into words. Mostly, I'm all for the "Show don't Tell" way of thinking. And when I'm writing these ideas I see in my mind so clearly, I have a very hard time showing stuff without the actual telling, since telling is a big part of writing. In one way or another, I have to "tell" stuff. Even simply describing in a non literal way some important but minute gesture, I feel like I'm forcing my readers to notice it, like I'm saying "Hey, look! See? They are angry." when in the case of movies, the camera doesn't need to zoom on that gesture for people to notice it. They only notice it if they happen to notice it and they interpret it as they feel right. Does any of this make sense? Does anyone have any tips? That's aren't the common "the character is frustrated? "They rolled their eyes"".



They receive the following reply to their post:

I love that you visualize your stories like movies. I mean, I visualize my meals like they're an action film. But let's be real, the big difference is no one's gonna smell bacon and start reading your fanfiction. Your problem sounds like every conversation I've had with my kids when they're trying to explain Minecraft to me. Seriously though, here's an idea: embrace the fact that writing is not film. It’s okay. Let readers in on the secret sauce without smacking them over the head with it. Explain it just enough so they get the vibe. Maybe try focusing on the big emotions and the stuff that impacts the story. Not every eyebrow raise or sideways glance needs a spotlight. And hey, if it all fails, there's a whole career in podcasting—no writing required!
